sender.en: A video or ad with the Prime Minister, a politician or a celebrity

name.en: Deepfake ad: “the Prime Minister recommends this investment”

how.en: An ad or video on Facebook, YouTube or another platform shows the Prime Minister, a politician or a well-known person promoting an investment, often crypto, saying it is safe or backed by the government. The video is AI-generated. After you sign up with a small amount, a “broker” calls you, shows fake profits on a website or app, and pushes you to invest more. When you try to withdraw, you are told to pay fees first, and the money is gone.

text.en: You see an ad or video of a famous person or politician promoting an investment.
It promises big, safe returns from a small first deposit.
A “broker” calls and shows your money growing on a trading website or app.
You are pushed to invest more, and asked for fees before you can withdraw.
BREAKING: Prime Minister reveals new platform that lets Canadians turn $350 into thousands every month. Government-backed and risk-free. Spots are limited, register today: [link]

en: ad backed by the bank of canada
broker called after i signed up
can't withdraw my money without fees
A public figure promotes an investment in an ad or video, or says it is government-backed.
Promises of high, guaranteed or risk-free returns.
Lip movement, voice or lighting that seems unnatural.
You must pay fees or taxes before withdrawing your money.
Assume investment videos of politicians and celebrities are fake.
Check that the company is registered with your provincial securities regulator before investing.
Never give a “broker” remote access to your device.
If you paid, call your bank, then report it to your local police and the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

sources.title: Watch out for AI-generated government impersonators
Ontario senior bilked out of $900K after falling victim to crypto scam that used AI deepfake of PM Carney

story.en: In 2025 an 86-year-old woman in Ontario saw a Facebook ad of the Prime Minister saying a $350 investment would be backed by the Bank of Canada. After she signed up, a caller said it had already tripled. Over the next months she put in everything she had, including a mortgage on her condo. Her account seemed to grow, but about $900,000 was gone, and the contact stopped after her last payment.
